nameStory: The gull-billed tern gets its name from its most distinctive feature - a thick, straight bill that looks remarkably like a seagull's beak rather than the thin, pointed bills of most other terns. This chunky bill gives it a completely different appearance from its needle-billed cousins, making it instantly recognizable once you know what to look for.
description: The gull-billed tern is a medium-sized seabird that's quite different from other terns you might see along New England's coast. It has a stocky build with broad wings, a short forked tail, and that signature thick, black bill that sets it apart from all other terns. In breeding plumage, adults have a crisp black cap on their heads and pale gray backs, while their underparts are clean white. They're roughly the size of a laughing gull, but with a more robust, powerful appearance.

idTips.label: Thick, straight bill
idTips.description: The bill is noticeably heavy and blunt, almost gull-like in appearance, completely different from the needle-sharp bills of other terns

idTips.label: Stocky build
idTips.description: Has a robust, chunky body that appears more muscular and broad-shouldered compared to the sleek, streamlined look of most terns

idTips.label: Short forked tail
idTips.description: The tail fork is much shallower than other terns - just a slight notch rather than the deep fork of common or least terns

idTips.label: Black cap in breeding
idTips.description: During breeding season, the entire top of the head from bill to nape is jet black, contrasting sharply with the white cheeks and neck

idTips.label: Pale gray upperparts
idTips.description: The back and wings are a soft, pearl-gray color that's lighter than most other terns, giving it an almost ghostly appearance in flight

idTips.label: Broad wings
idTips.description: Wings appear wider and more rounded than other terns, giving it a more gull-like flight profile with slower, more deliberate wingbeats

habitat: In New England, gull-billed terns are most likely found around salt marshes, shallow coastal bays, and barrier beaches where they can hunt for insects and small fish. They prefer areas with mix of open water and marshy edges, often seen flying over spartina grass flats and tidal pools. Unlike other terns that stick close to open ocean, gull-billed terns venture inland over salt marshes and even freshwater ponds near the coast.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring migrants may appear in late April or May, usually in full breeding plumage with crisp black caps and gray backs.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for sightings in New England, though still uncommon. Adults in full breeding plumage may be seen hunting over salt marshes and coastal waters from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Occasional fall migrants pass through in September, often showing mixed plumage as they molt out of breeding colors, with patchy black caps.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter; any gull-billed terns would show pale gray caps with dark ear patches instead of the full black breeding cap.

funFact: Unlike most terns that dive headfirst into water to catch fish, gull-billed terns often hunt like flycatchers, swooping down to snatch insects, frogs, and even small crabs right off the surface of marsh grass or sand - they're basically the Swiss Army knife of the tern world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Forster's tern, but the gull-billed tern's thick, blunt bill is the dead giveaway - if you can imagine a tern trying to eat with a butter knife instead of a steak knife, that's the gull-billed tern. Forster's terns have the typical long, thin, pointed tern bill and a much more deeply forked tail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'tern,' the gull-billed tern's behavior is quite different from its relatives - it rarely dives for fish like other terns do, instead picking food from surfaces more like a gull would. This has led some birders to joke that it's having an identity crisis, not quite sure if it wants to be a gull or a tern!
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in our region, gull-billed tern is most easily compared to other medium-sized terns in the Laridae family. Compared to common terns, it's bulkier with that distinctive thick bill and shorter tail fork. Compared to Forster's tern, it has a much heavier build and completely different bill shape. The combination of stocky body, thick bill, and pale coloration makes it unique among New England terns.
